new.title: Watch the Glockenspiel joust on Marienplatz
new.desc: High on the Neues Rathaus, 43 bells ring while life-size figures replay a ducal wedding of 1568, complete with a tournament the Bavarian knight always wins, followed by the coopers' dance.
new.tip: Stand back towards the Mariensäule for the best angle. The late evening show, when a night watchman and the Münchner Kindl are sent to bed, draws far fewer people.

new.title: Step into the devil's footprint in the Frauenkirche
new.desc: Just inside the cathedral entrance a dark footprint with a spur mark is set in the floor. Legend says the devil stamped here in glee because, from this spot, the pillars hide every window.
new.tip: Stand on the print and check the legend for yourself, then take the stairs and lift up the south tower for a glassed-in view over the old town.

new.title: Squeeze into the Asamkirche
new.desc: Two artist brothers built this tiny late Baroque church next to their own house and covered every surface in gold, stucco and fresco. One of them could see the high altar from his bedroom window.
new.tip: Come in the morning, when daylight reaches the dark interior, and look up for the figures above the altar lit by hidden windows.

new.title: Follow the bronze trail through the Viscardigasse
new.desc: Locals call this lane the Drückebergergasserl, or shirkers' alley. In the Nazi years people cut through here to avoid saluting a memorial at the Feldherrnhalle, and a winding line of bronze cobbles remembers their quiet refusal.
new.tip: The Feldherrnhalle itself is under scaffolding for a long renovation, so the alley behind it is currently the more rewarding stop.

new.title: Step from yellow into white at the Theatinerkirche
new.desc: The butter-yellow Baroque church on Odeonsplatz was built to celebrate the birth of a long-awaited heir. Behind the sunny facade the interior is a surprise: entirely white stucco under a dome some 70 metres high.
new.tip: Sightseeing pauses during services. The Wittelsbach crypt below can be combined with the one at St. Michael on a joint ticket.

new.title: Find Ludwig II's coffin under St. Michael
new.desc: The Jesuit church on the main shopping street has a vast barrel vault that spans the nave without a single column. In the crypt below lies the fairy-tale king Ludwig II, his coffin usually covered in fresh flowers from admirers.
new.tip: The crypt entrance is at the front right of the church, down a flight of stairs. It stays shut on Sundays and public holidays.

new.title: Watch the river surfers on the Eisbach
new.desc: Right where the Eisbach shoots out from under Prinzregentenstraße, surfers in wetsuits queue on both banks to ride a standing wave in the middle of the city, in every season.
new.tip: After a long closure the wave was released for surfing again in spring 2026, for experienced surfers only. Watch from the bridge, keep the banks clear and leave your bike elsewhere, the spot is narrow.

new.title: Sit on the Glyptothek steps at Königsplatz
new.desc: King Ludwig I wanted an Athens on the Isar, and this square of temples and a monumental gate is the result. It also has a dark chapter as a Nazi parade ground, which the documentation centre nearby explains.
new.tip: The steps of the Glyptothek catch the sun until evening and are a favourite spot for sunset watchers. In summer the square hosts big open-air concerts.

new.title: Visit the unofficial Michael Jackson shrine
new.desc: The statue on Promenadeplatz honours Renaissance composer Orlando di Lasso, but since 2009 its base has been covered in photos, candles and flowers for Michael Jackson. He used to stay at the Bayerischer Hof opposite, and fans waited here for him to appear at a window.
new.tip: It is tended by fans, so the decoration changes all the time. Look across to the hotel to see what they were all staring at.

new.title: Find the six folk singers on the Viktualienmarkt
new.desc: Scattered between the market stalls are six small fountains, each topped by a beloved Munich comedian or folk singer such as Karl Valentin and Liesl Karlstadt. Valentin's contains bronze from a war-damaged lion of the Siegestor.
new.tip: Market people often tuck fresh flowers into the figures' hands. On the first Friday of August the fountains are decorated for the Brunnenfest, with free performances.

new.title: Cool off by the Wittelsbacherbrunnen
new.desc: Munich's grandest fountain sits where Lenbachplatz meets Maximiliansplatz. Its monumental stone figures are an allegory of the elemental forces of water, and the calm, clear design is rated among the finest of its era.
new.tip: It is most impressive lit up after dark. The Alter Botanischer Garten, now a public park, is a short walk west.

new.title: Walk through the Sendlinger Tor
new.desc: One of three medieval city gates still standing, the brick Sendlinger Tor marks the southern edge of the old town. It came through the war almost unharmed, a rarity in central Munich.
new.tip: In summer the huge fountain on the square outside is switched on. From the gate, Sendlinger Straße leads past the Asamkirche towards Marienplatz.

new.title: Wander the Alter Nordfriedhof
new.desc: Burials stopped here in the 1940s and the walled cemetery has since turned into one of Maxvorstadt's most loved green spaces, where weathered gravestones share the grounds with joggers and people reading on benches.
new.tip: It is a quiet retreat between museum visits. Enter from Arcisstraße and remember that it is still a cemetery.

new.title: Stand under the giant fresco in the Ludwigskirche
new.desc: The twin-towered university church on Ludwigstraße holds what counts as the second largest altar fresco in the world. The building itself was the first monumental church in the round-arch style.
new.tip: It stands opposite the main university building, so it combines well with the White Rose memorial across the road.

new.title: Remember the White Rose at Geschwister-Scholl-Platz
new.desc: The square in front of the university is named after Hans and Sophie Scholl, who were arrested here in 1943 after scattering leaflets against the Nazi regime in the atrium. A memorial exhibition beside the Lichthof tells the resistance group's story.
new.tip: Look for the leaflets set into the paving outside the entrance, then walk into the main building and find the DenkStätte by the Lichthof.

new.title: Walk the length of the Antiquarium in the Residenz
new.desc: The oldest room of the Wittelsbach palace is a painted Renaissance hall almost 66 metres long, built for the ducal collection of antiquities. It is the showpiece of a museum that also takes in a shell-encrusted grotto courtyard and the Bavarian crown in the Schatzkammer.
new.tip: The palace is enormous, so allow a couple of hours and pick up the audio guide included with your ticket.

new.title: Find the Large Red Sphere in the Türkentor
new.desc: The Türkentor is the last fragment of a royal infantry barracks, stranded between the modern museums. Inside the bare gatehouse sits Walter De Maria's Large Red Sphere, and nothing else.
new.tip: It is a two-minute stop between the Pinakothek der Moderne and Museum Brandhorst, home to Warhol and Cy Twombly.

new.title: Raise a Maß in the Hofbräuhaus Schwemme
new.desc: The world's best-known beer hall is touristy and great fun anyway. The Schwemme is the vast ground-floor hall where the brewery once stood, with long shared tables and oompah music.
new.tip: Just take any free seat at a shared table and say hello to your neighbours. The upper floors are calmer than the Schwemme.

new.title: Master Weißwurst etiquette at the Weisses Bräuhaus
new.desc: The Schneider wheat-beer tavern in the Tal is a proper setting for Munich's breakfast ritual: veal sausages, sweet mustard, a Brezn and a Weißbier. Tradition says the sausage must never hear the noon bells.
new.tip: Never eat the skin. Either cut the sausage open and peel it, or zuzeln, which means sucking the meat out of the casing. Go mid-morning.

new.title: Drink Augustiner at its Stammhaus
new.desc: Augustiner is the city's oldest brewery, and its beer hall and restaurant on the pedestrian street is the classic place to try it, with plenty of atmosphere and traditional Bavarian cooking.
new.tip: It gets busy with shoppers at lunchtime. Mid-afternoon is the easiest time to find a table.

new.title: Have a beer under the chestnuts on the Viktualienmarkt
new.desc: The only beer garden in the old town sits in the middle of the food market. The six big Munich breweries take turns at the tap every few weeks, and a sign at the bar says whose beer is flowing.
new.tip: You may bring your own Brotzeit, so shop for cheese, radishes and Brezn at the stalls first and buy only the drinks here.

new.title: Order Rostbratwürstl at the Bratwurst Glöckl
new.desc: This traditional tavern opposite the Frauenkirche specialises in little Nürnberger grilled sausages. They are smaller than usual, so a portion is six rather than three.
new.tip: The tables outside face the cathedral and fill up fast on sunny days.
new.q: Nürnberger Bratwurst Glöckl am Dom München

new.title: Browse the delicatessen halls at Dallmayr
new.desc: Germany's most famous delicatessen has been feeding Munich since around 1700 and draws millions of visitors a year to its counters. The café-bistro upstairs serves a refined Weißwurst breakfast.
new.tip: The Weißwurst breakfast is a morning-only affair. Otherwise, a bag of the house coffee makes an easy souvenir.

new.title: Eat a hot Schmalznudel at Café Frischhut
new.desc: Everyone just calls this place the Schmalznudel, after the pastry it fries fresh in front of you: a disc of yeast dough also known as an Auszogne, served hot and dusted with sugar. The Frischhut family has run it since the 1970s.
new.tip: Order one straight from the pan with a coffee, to eat in the wood-panelled room or take away. It is closed on Sundays.

new.title: Have cake at Café Luitpold
new.desc: Opened in 1888 as one of the grand coffee houses of its age and rebuilt after the war, the Luitpold is still the place in Munich for a proper slice of torte in elegant surroundings.
new.tip: Go up to the first floor, where a small museum tells the story of the café.

new.title: Sink into the 1950s at Café Jasmin
new.desc: The interior of this Maxvorstadt café is largely original 1950s and now a listed monument. Students and regulars come for homemade cake and hot chocolate in retro comfort.
new.tip: It is popular for weekend breakfast, so come on a weekday afternoon if you want your pick of the seats.

new.title: Eat with the students at the Alter Simpl
new.desc: This traditional pub in the university quarter has long had a student and arty crowd. It is a Maxvorstadt institution for a beer and a plate of something hearty.
new.tip: It sits on Türkenstraße, the liveliest street of the quarter, so it works well as the start or end of a bar crawl.

new.title: Drink Palatinate wine inside the Residenz
new.desc: In beer-mad Munich, the Pfälzer Residenz Weinstube pours no beer at all. It occupies rooms in the royal palace and is said to be Germany's largest wine tavern, serving only wines from the Palatinate with regional dishes to match.
new.tip: It faces Odeonsplatz, next to the Feldherrnhalle. Order by the Schoppen, the generous Palatinate measure.

new.title: Sip a cocktail in the Goldene Bar
new.desc: Tucked into the Haus der Kunst, this bar is wrapped in gold-leaf wall paintings from 1937 showing where rum, whisky, champagne and tobacco come from. They were boarded over after the war and uncovered again decades later.
new.tip: It also serves lunch and afternoon coffee and cake. In fine weather sit on the terrace at the back, a few steps from the Eisbach surfers.
new.q: Goldene Bar Haus der Kunst München

new.title: Have a drink at the Minna Thiel railbus
new.desc: In the Kunstareal, an old railbus, a cargo container and a phone booth have been turned into a small canopied beer garden with DJs and live music. It is the museum quarter's most relaxed place for a drink.
new.tip: Many of the culture events are free, so check what is on before you go.

new.title: Climb the Alter Peter
new.desc: About 300 steps lead up the tower of Munich's oldest parish church to a viewing platform with the classic panorama: Marienplatz, the Frauenkirche towers and the old town roofs, with the Alps on a clear Föhn day.
new.tip: There is no advance booking, so go early or late. Inside the church, look for the relics of St. Munditia in a glass coffin.

new.title: Meet the Old Masters in the Alte Pinakothek
new.desc: One of the world's great galleries, with European masterworks from the 14th to the 18th century and the largest Rubens collection anywhere.
new.tip: Sunday admission is a small fraction of the weekday price. Café Klenze inside is a pleasant stop, and the lawn outside is a neighbourhood meeting place.

new.title: See four museums in one at the Pinakothek der Moderne
new.desc: Under one roof you get four independent museums: modern art, works on paper, architecture and Die Neue Sammlung, a major design collection.
new.tip: Give the design museum plenty of time. Sundays are heavily discounted here too.

new.title: Find the Blue Horse in the Lenbachhaus
new.desc: A painter prince's Italianate villa with a striking modern extension holds the world's largest collection of the Blaue Reiter group, including Franz Marc's blue horse and works by Kandinsky, Klee and Macke.
new.tip: The garden and Lenbach's historic studio rooms can be visited without a ticket. Café Ella has a terrace looking towards Königsplatz.

new.title: Walk among marble gods in the Glyptothek
new.desc: Ludwig I, determined to turn Munich into a new Athens, built this temple-like museum for his huge collection of Greek and Roman sculpture, including the figures from the temple of Aegina.
new.tip: A good choice for a rainy hour. The Antikensammlungen across the square continue the story with Greek vases and jewellery.

new.title: Face the past at the NS-Dokumentationszentrum
new.desc: This documentation centre stands on the site of the former Nazi party headquarters and records how the movement grew up in Munich and what followed, naming the perpetrators and their acts.
new.tip: Admission is free. The exhibition is text-heavy, with translations, so give it time.

new.title: Climb the Himmelsleiter in the Bier- und Oktoberfestmuseum
new.desc: An old Munich townhouse dating from the 14th century tells the story of beer and of the Oktoberfest. Its early staircase, the Himmelsleiter or stairway to heaven, runs up in one straight flight with no corners.
new.tip: The museum is run by the foundation behind the Augustiner brewery, so expect the beer history to be told with some pride.

new.title: Get the jokes at the Valentin-Karlstadt-Musäum
new.desc: The towers of the medieval Isartor house a deliberately quirky museum for comedian Karl Valentin and his stage partner Liesl Karlstadt, full of absurd exhibits.
new.tip: Climb to the Turmstüberl café in the tower, where Weißwürste are served from late morning.

new.title: Play billiards at the Schelling-Salon
new.desc: This Viennese-style café and pub has stood on Schellingstraße since 1872 and kept much of its interior. Brecht, Kandinsky and Rilke were guests, and Hitler is said to have moved on after running up unpaid bills. People still come for the pool and carom tables.
new.tip: There are table tennis tables in the basement as well. Tables can be booked online, which is wise on weekend evenings.

new.title: Watch the boules players in the Hofgarten
new.desc: The court garden behind the Residenz was laid out in the 17th century on Italian lines, with eight paths meeting at the Dianatempel. Boules players hold their own tournaments on the gravel, and dancers and musicians use the pavilion as a stage.
new.tip: Walk the arcades too, which are painted with scenes from Wittelsbach history.

new.title: Watch a tea ceremony at the Japanese teahouse
new.desc: On a small artificial island in the Schwabinger Bach, at the southern end of the Englischer Garten, stands a Japanese teahouse built for the 1972 Olympics. In the warm months it hosts public demonstrations of the traditional tea ceremony.
new.tip: Demonstrations run from April to October on selected dates, so check first. A Japanfest fills the lawns around it in July.

new.title: Stroll the Christkindlmarkt on Marienplatz
new.desc: Munich's main Christmas market spreads around a tree almost 30 metres tall in front of the Rathaus, with some 140 stalls and a programme of music.
new.tip: It draws millions of visitors, so come on a weekday and warm your hands on a mug of Glühwein.

new.title: Cheer the dancing market women on Shrove Tuesday
new.desc: The high point of Munich's street carnival comes on the morning of Faschingsdienstag, when the women who run the Viktualienmarkt stalls perform their rehearsed dances in costume.
new.tip: The dance starts in the late morning and the square is packed well before, so come early.

new.title: Hear an orchestra at Klassik am Odeonsplatz
new.desc: For two evenings each July the square between the Theatinerkirche and the Residenz becomes an open-air concert hall, with the Munich Philharmonic, the Bavarian Radio Symphony Orchestra and international guests.
new.tip: Check the dates and ticket arrangements well in advance, as this is one of the highlights of the Munich summer.
